  "title": "TemporalProbe: Which Internal Signal Best Detects Hallucination Onset? A Controlled Comparison of Attention Sinks, Hidden States, and Log-Probabilities as Temporal Features",
  "core_problem": "Multiple internal LLM signals — attention sink scores, hidden-state spectral features, and log-probabilities — have each been independently shown to be effective for hallucination detection when modeled temporally (SinkProbe achieves 23/28 model-dataset wins with static attention sinks; EigenTrack reaches 0.82–0.94 AUROC with GRU-based hidden-state tracking; HALT detects hallucination via GRU on log-probability time series; HSAD gains >10 AUROC points via FFT on cross-layer hidden signals). Yet these results are incomparable: each method uses different architectures, training data, evaluation protocols, and model-benchmark combinations. No systematic comparison exists that isolates the signal modality as the independent variable — training identical temporal classifiers on parallel feature streams extracted from the same generations under the same evaluation protocol. This means the field cannot answer a basic question: which internal temporal signal is earliest, strongest, and most reliable for detecting hallucination during generation? This gap has practical consequences: practitioners building real-time hallucination guardrails must choose a signal type (attention patterns, hidden states, or output logits) with no principled basis for the choice, and researchers proposing new temporal detectors cannot claim superiority without a controlled cross-signal baseline. Furthermore, temporal modeling has never been applied to the strongest known attention-based feature (attention sink scores from SinkProbe), meaning an entire arm of the comparison space is untested. Adjacent temporal approaches target different signals or domains: RAUQ (arXiv 2505.20045) recurrently aggregates generic attention weights at sequence granularity without a learned temporal model; TDGNet (arXiv 2602.08048) tracks temporal attention graphs but only in diffusion language models; TARAC (arXiv 2504.04099) tracks temporal visual attention in VLMs for hallucination mitigation, not detection in text LLMs; HSAD (arXiv 2509.13154) applies FFT to cross-layer hidden-state signals (vertical dynamics across layers) rather than cross-step temporal dynamics during generation; MIND (ACL Findings 2024, arXiv 2403.06448) detects hallucination from last-layer hidden-state embeddings unsupervisedly but operates post-generation, not during generation, and uses a single snapshot rather than temporal modeling.",
  "opportunity": "Three independent research threads have converged to make this comparison both possible and timely. (1) Feature identification: SinkProbe (arXiv 2604.10697) established attention sink scores as the strongest attention-based hallucination signal via logistic regression on per-head sink features, using ℓ₁ regularization in its interpretability analysis (Section 4.1) to identify the most informative head-layer combinations. (2) Temporal architecture: EigenTrack (arXiv 2509.15735) and HALT (arXiv 2602.02888) independently proved that lightweight GRU classifiers on per-step internal features achieve strong hallucination detection — but on hidden-state spectral features and log-probabilities respectively, never on attention patterns. (3) Causal grounding: SinkTrack (ICLR 2026) demonstrated that modifying attention sinks causally affects hallucination rates, and FACTUM (arXiv 2601.05866) showed that correct vs. hallucinated citations differ specifically in attention sink usage patterns — establishing that sinks carry independent hallucination-relevant information, not merely downstream reflections of hidden-state dynamics. The key insight: these threads define a natural factorial experiment. We have three validated signal types (attention sinks, hidden states, log-probs), one validated temporal architecture (GRU), and shared evaluation infrastructure. By training identical GRU classifiers on parallel feature streams extracted from the same model generations, we can isolate the signal modality as the sole independent variable. This controlled comparison — the first of its kind — is the primary contribution. As part of this comparison, we introduce SinkWatch-GRU, the attention-sink arm that fills the untested cell: a GRU temporal detector consuming per-step attention sink features from SinkProbe's informative heads. Whether attention sinks win, lose, or tie in the comparison, the systematic evaluation constitutes a rigorous empirical contribution that provides the missing evidence base for signal selection in temporal hallucination detection.",
  "landscape": "**Attention-based hallucination detection (static):** SinkProbe (arXiv 2604.10697, April 2026) proved sink scores outperform spectral Laplacian eigenvalues in 23/28 model-dataset pairs via logistic regression on attention sink features (AUROC 0.778 on TruthfulQA, 0.890 on HaluEval-QA for Llama-3.1-8B), with ℓ₁-regularized variant used for interpretability to identify informative heads. LapEigvals (EMNLP 2025, arXiv 2502.17598) established spectral attention features as hallucination signals. CHARM (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2509.24770) applies GNNs on attributed attention graphs combining attention and activation features. Spectral Guardrails (arXiv 2602.08082, Feb 2026) achieves 97.7% recall via training-free spectral attention topology analysis. AggTruth (ICCS 2025, arXiv 2506.18628) aggregates attention scores with windowing. TOHA (ACL 2026, arXiv 2504.10063) uses topological divergence on attention graphs. Frequency-Aware Attention (arXiv 2602.18145) shows high-frequency attention energy correlates with hallucination. FACTUM (arXiv 2601.05866) uses attention sink usage as one of four mechanistic signals. **All compute features from static snapshots; none model attention feature trajectories across generation steps.**\n\n**Temporal/trajectory hallucination analysis:** Hallucination as Trajectory Commitment (arXiv 2604.15400, April 2026) provides causal evidence that residual-stream trajectories bifurcate at the first generated token in 44.3% of prompts on Qwen2.5-1.5B, with asymmetric attractor dynamics — but tested only residual-stream activations on a single small model, not attention patterns. Before the First Token (arXiv 2604.13068) demonstrates scale-dependent emergence of hallucination signals at position zero. Hallucination Basins (arXiv 2604.04743) formalizes hallucination as trajectory capture in latent-space basins. HalluSAE (arXiv 2604.16430) models hallucination as phase transitions in latent dynamics via sparse autoencoders. Attractor Geometry (arXiv 2605.05686, May 2026) models facts as attractor basins in hidden-state space. First Hallucination Tokens (arXiv 2507.20836) shows the first hallucinated token is far more detectable. Shadows in the Attention (arXiv 2505.16894) reveals an 'attention-locking' threshold (JS-Drift ~0.69) — but tracks drift across prompt perturbation rounds, not generation steps. Step-Level Hallucination Detection via Hidden-State Transport Geometry (arXiv 2605.13772, May 2026) frames hallucination as localized excursion in transport cost along hidden-state trajectories, using BiLSTM on geometric transition features — exclusively on hidden states, not attention. **All study residual-stream or mixed-modality dynamics; none systematically compare signal modalities under controlled conditions.**\n\n**Temporal feature tracking for detection (methods):** EigenTrack (arXiv 2509.15735, 2025) tracks temporal spectral dynamics of hidden-state covariance via GRU (0.82–0.94 AUROC). HALT (arXiv 2602.02888, Feb 2026) treats log-probs as time series via bidirectional GRU (hidden_dim=256, 5 layers). HSAD (arXiv 2509.13154, Sep 2025) applies FFT to cross-layer hidden-state activations, achieving 82.5% AUROC on TruthfulQA and 92.1% on TriviaQA for Qwen-2.5-7B — conceptually related but models vertical dynamics (across layers within a single step) rather than horizontal dynamics (across generation steps). TDGNet (arXiv 2602.08048) targets diffusion language models only. ICR Probe (ACL 2025, arXiv 2507.16488) tracks cross-layer hidden-state evolution (0.73–0.84 AUROC). **Each validates temporal modeling for one signal type but no paper compares signal types under identical temporal architectures.**\n\n**Real-time/online detection:** MIND (ACL Findings 2024, arXiv 2403.06448) is the foundational real-time internal-state detector: an unsupervised framework using last-layer contextualized embeddings with an MLP, achieving passage-level AUC 0.89–0.96 with only 3.3% overhead — but operates post-generation on the final hidden state, uses no temporal modeling, and does not leverage attention patterns. PCNet/PC-LDCD (arXiv 2605.05953, May 2026) trains probabilistic circuits on hidden-state residual stream for online detection (AUROC reaching up to 0.99 on CoQA/SQuAD, but 0.66–0.81 on TruthfulQA). RAUQ (arXiv 2505.20045) identifies 'uncertainty-aware' attention heads and recurrently aggregates weights for sequence-level uncertainty — uses simple aggregation (not learned temporal model), targets generic attention (not sinks), operates at sequence granularity. DRIFT (arXiv 2601.14210) trains lightweight probes on hidden states (<0.1% overhead, SOTA on 10/12 settings). Real-Time Entity Detection (arXiv 2509.03531) achieves AUC 0.90 via linear probes on hidden states. Streaming Hallucination Detection (arXiv 2601.02170) treats step-level hallucination as evolving latent state. Monitoring Decoding (ACL Findings 2025, arXiv 2503.03106) uses external reference model logits with 5.7× overhead. **All use hidden-state, logit, or generic attention features; none apply learned temporal models to attention sink features, and none compare signal modalities.**\n\n**Attention sink context:** Attention Sink Survey (arXiv 2604.10098) reviews 180+ papers. SinkTrack (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2604.10027) converts passive attention sinks into active context anchors — demonstrating causal relevance. TARAC (arXiv 2504.04099) tracks visual attention decay in VLMs for mitigation. Mirage in the Eyes (USENIX Security 2025, arXiv 2501.15269) exploits sinks for adversarial attacks.\n\n**The open gap:** (1) No controlled comparison exists of temporal detection performance across attention sinks, hidden states, and log-probabilities as feature modalities using identical architectures, training data, and evaluation. (2) No method applies learned temporal modeling to attention sink features during autoregressive text generation.",
  "approach": "We propose TemporalProbe, a controlled experimental framework for comparing which internal temporal signal — attention sinks, hidden-state spectral features, or log-probabilities — is most informative for detecting hallucination during autoregressive generation. The framework trains identical GRU classifiers on parallel feature streams extracted from the same model generations, isolating the signal modality as the independent variable. As part of this comparison, we introduce SinkWatch-GRU, the first learned temporal detector on attention sink features, filling the untested cell in the comparison.\n\n**Experimental Framework: Three Parallel Arms.** For each generation, we extract three parallel feature streams at every decoding step t:\n\n*Arm 1 — SinkWatch (Attention Sinks):* Per-step features from the top-K informative head-layer combinations (K=5–15) identified via SinkProbe's ℓ₁-regularized interpretability analysis: (a) sink scores for top-k sink tokens (k=2–3), (b) sink concentration (max sink / total sink), (c) sink entropy, (d) context-attention ratio. Augmented with first-order temporal derivatives. Dimensionality ~50–120.\n\n*Arm 2 — EigenTrack-style (Hidden States):* Per-step spectral features from sliding-window covariance matrices of hidden-state activations: leading eigenvalues, spectral gaps, entropy, and RMT statistics. Matching EigenTrack's feature design.\n\n*Arm 3 — HALT-style (Log-Probabilities):* Per-step log-probability features: token log-prob, predictive entropy, top-k probability gap, rank. Matching HALT's feature design.\n\nAll three streams feed into identical unidirectional GRUs (hidden_dim=64, ~25K parameters each), trained with identical binary cross-entropy loss, hyperparameters, and data splits. This controlled design isolates the feature modality — same architecture, same training data, same evaluation.\n\n**Primary Analysis: Cross-Signal Comparison.** (1) Detection performance: AUROC and AUPRC for each signal arm at sequence level. (2) Early-detection curves: AUROC as a function of the fraction of the response observed (at 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of tokens), testing which signal enables earliest detection. (3) Temporal lead/lag analysis: measuring when each signal first shows significant distributional shift relative to annotated hallucination onset. (4) Complementarity: late-fusion ensemble combining all three streams to test whether signals carry redundant or orthogonal information; mutual information analysis between per-step predictions from each arm. (5) Ablation: SinkWatch-GRU vs. SinkWatch-LR (logistic regression on windowed features) to quantify the benefit of learned temporal modeling over simple aggregation.\n\n**Temporal Characterization (Supporting Analysis).** Statistical tests (paired t-test, Kolmogorov-Smirnov) on sink feature distributions at and before annotated hallucination onset points for 500 examples with entity-match-based onset annotation. This provides the first empirical evidence on whether attention sink features exhibit gradual drift (enabling temporal detection) or abrupt bifurcation (matching the Trajectory Commitment paper's finding for residual-stream activations).\n\n**Intervention (Extension, AAAI 2027 only).** When the best-performing arm's running probability exceeds a high-confidence threshold, trigger DoLa contrastive decoding for subsequent tokens. Evaluate hallucination rate reduction.\n\n**Planned Pilot (First 48 hours).** Before full-scale experiments, run a 2-hour pilot on 100 TruthfulQA examples with Llama-3.1-8B: extract per-step sink features, plot distributions for factual vs. hallucinated tokens at generation fractions (25/50/75/100%). This provides the first empirical evidence for or against the temporal hypothesis before committing to full compute.\n\n**Dual-Target Venue Strategy:**\n\n*EMNLP 2026 (ARR May 25 — short paper, 4 pages):* Radically descoped. 1 model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), 1 benchmark (TruthfulQA, matching SinkProbe), 1K examples, entity-match onset annotation. Focus: cross-signal comparison (3 arms) + SinkWatch-GRU vs. static SinkProbe + early-detection curves. Key result: which temporal signal is strongest/earliest for hallucination detection. No intervention experiments, no 70B model.\n\n*AAAI 2027 (full paper, 8 pages):* Complete framework. 3 models (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Llama-3.1-70B), 3 benchmarks (TruthfulQA, TriviaQA, HaluEval-QA), 2K examples per pair. Full cross-signal comparison, temporal characterization, complementarity analysis, DoLa intervention, comprehensive ablations.\n\n**Training and Evaluation.** Generate outputs, annotate with binary factual/hallucinated labels via NLI against gold references (validated by manual spot-check of 200 examples), split 70/15/15. For EMNLP short paper: simplified entity-match annotation on TruthfulQA only.\n\n**Baselines.** Static: SinkProbe, LapEigvals, TOHA. Temporal: EigenTrack, HALT. Online: MIND (unsupervised hidden-state), DRIFT, RAUQ, PCNet. Ablation: SinkWatch-LR.\n\n**Evaluation Metrics.** Primary: AUROC and AUPRC. Secondary: early-detection AUROC at partial observation, F1 at calibrated threshold, latency overhead (ms/token), mutual information between arms. For intervention (AAAI only): hallucination rate reduction and fluency preservation.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 5)
Issues: ["MISSING COMPETING WORK — HALUPROBE (arXiv 2502.13490, Feb 2025): 'What are Models Thinking about? Understanding Large Language Model Hallucinations through Model Inner State Analysis' systematically compares attention weights, hidden states, and logits for hallucination detection across three inference stages on HaluEval and CNNDM. While it uses static classifiers (not temporal GRU models) and only tests Llama-2-7B/Vicuna-7B, it IS a systematic signal-type comparison for hallucination detection and must be cited and differentiated. Conclusion from HALUPROBE: 'attention-based features provide more consistent performance across datasets' — directly relevant to TemporalProbe's hypothesis.", "MISSING COMPETING WORK — UniFact (arXiv 2512.02772, Dec 2025): Unified evaluation framework that dynamically generates model outputs and corresponding factuality labels, enabling direct instance-level comparison between hallucination detection and fact verification methods. Relevant as a comparison framework for internal-signal methods.", "PCNet AUROC MISREPRESENTED: Proposal claims '0.91–0.98 AUROC' without dataset qualification. On TruthfulQA specifically (TemporalProbe's EMNLP benchmark), PCNet achieves only 0.66–0.81 AUROC across models (0.75 for Llama-3.1-8B). The 0.99 figure applies to CoQA/SQuAD only. This misrepresentation actually HURTS the proposal — the real PCNet-on-TruthfulQA baseline is much weaker than claimed, which is favorable for TemporalProbe.", "ENTITY-MATCH ANNOTATION LIMITATION UNACKNOWLEDGED: TruthfulQA tests nuanced factual claims (e.g., 'What happens if you swallow gum?' — correct answer involves no harm, but entity matching won't capture this). Entity-match onset annotation will be unreliable for many TruthfulQA questions. The proposal should discuss this limitation and its impact on temporal lead/lag analysis reliability.", "TRAJECTORY COMMITMENT COUNTER-EVIDENCE: The pilot in 48 hours is a reasonable mitigation, but the proposal should explicitly state the decision rule: if the pilot shows abrupt sink feature bifurcation (matching arXiv 2604.15400's findings for residual stream), the temporal GRU may offer no advantage over static SinkProbe on the same features. In that case, the paper's contribution reduces to the cross-signal comparison only. This should be acknowledged upfront.", "HALUPROBE PARTIALLY SUBSUMES NOVELTY CLAIM: HALUPROBE found 'attention-based features provide more consistent performance across datasets' using static classifiers. If TemporalProbe's GRU-based comparison reaches the same conclusion (attention features are best), the temporal modeling adds limited insight beyond confirming HALUPROBE's static finding with a more expensive method. The proposal should preemptively address this by emphasizing what temporal modeling reveals that static comparison cannot: early-detection curves, temporal lead/lag, and complementarity — these are the unique contributions."]
Feedback: The proposal is close to passing but needs three specific fixes:

1. **Cite HALUPROBE (arXiv 2502.13490) and differentiate.** HALUPROBE already compares attention, hidden states, and logits for hallucination detection (statically) and finds attention features most consistent. Your paper must cite this and argue why temporal comparison reveals insights static comparison cannot — specifically: (a) early-detection curves at partial observation, (b) temporal lead/lag analysis at hallucination onset, (c) whether the ranking changes when signals are modeled temporally vs. statically. Frame TemporalProbe as 'HALUPROBE showed attention wins statically; we test whether this ranking holds when signals are modeled as temporal sequences during generation.'

2. **Correct PCNet's TruthfulQA AUROC.** Report 0.66–0.81 for TruthfulQA (0.75 for Llama-3.1-8B) and note the 0.99 figure applies to other benchmarks. This actually strengthens your positioning — TruthfulQA is harder for all methods, making your comparison more meaningful.

3. **Acknowledge entity-match annotation limitations** for TruthfulQA and discuss how this affects temporal analysis reliability. Consider whether a subset of TruthfulQA questions with clear entity-based answers could be selected for the temporal lead/lag analysis specifically.

These are minor revisions — the core proposal is sound.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，

## HALUPROBE: Detailed Research Report

**Full Title:** "What are Models Thinking about? Understanding Large Language Model Hallucinations 'Psychology' through Model Inner State Analysis"

**arXiv:** 2502.13490 (submitted February 19, 2025)

**Authors:** Peiran Wang (UCLA, PhD student under Prof. Yuan Tian), Yang Liu, Yunfei Lu, Jue Hong, Ye Wu

**Fields:** cs.CL (Computation and Language), cs.AI (Artificial Intelligence)

---

### 1. ABSTRACT (verbatim)

> "Large language model (LLM) systems suffer from the models' unstable ability to generate valid and factual content, resulting in hallucination generation. Current hallucination detection methods heavily rely on out-of-model information sources, such as RAG to assist the detection, thus bringing heavy additional latency. Recently, internal states of LLMs' inference have been widely used in numerous research works, such as prompt injection detection, etc. Considering the interpretability of LLM internal states and the fact that they do not require external information sources, we introduce such states into LLM hallucination detection. In this paper, we systematically analyze different internal states' revealing features during inference forward and comprehensively evaluate their ability in hallucination detection. Specifically, we cut the forward process of a large language model into three stages: understanding, query, generation, and extracting the internal state from these stages. By analyzing these states, we provide a deep understanding of why the hallucinated content is generated and what happened in the internal state of the models. Then, we introduce these internal states into hallucination detection and conduct comprehensive experiments to discuss the advantages and limitations."

---

### 2. THE THREE INFERENCE STAGES

HaluProbe divides an LLM's forward pass into three sequential stages:

1. **Understanding Stage** -- Processes input tokens through multi-head self-attention mechanisms to generate contextual representations. Attention is extracted as the internal state in which LLMs "understand the input context," and attention score matrices are extracted from each transformer layer's head for each token.

2. **Query Stage** -- Further processes contextual representations through feedforward networks (FFNs) to extract higher-level abstractions. Involves linear transformation (`z_{l,t} = W_1 * gamma_{l,t} + b_1`) followed by non-linear activation (`a_{l,t} = GELU(z_{l,t})`).

3. **Generation Stage** -- Converts query outputs into probability distributions for the next token through linear transformation and softmax. This produces the logit-based signals.

---

### 3. SIGNAL TYPES COMPARED

Three categories of internal signals, corresponding to the three stages:

- **Attention states** (Understanding stage)
- **Activation / hidden states** (Query stage)
- **Logit states** (Generation stage)

---

### 4. THE 8 EXTRACTED FEATURES

**Attention-based (from Understanding stage):**
1. **Attention Lookback Ratio** -- "the proportion of attention score directed to previous tokens among all attention scores for that token: `sum_{i<t} alpha_{l,h,i->t} / sum_j alpha_{l,h,j->t}`"
2. **Attention Allocation Sharpness (Entropy)** -- `- sum_j p_{l,h,j->t} log p_{l,h,j->t}` where `p_{l,h,j->t} = alpha_{l,h,j->t} / sum_k alpha_{l,h,k->t}`
3. **Key Token Attention Ratio** -- Appears in results but formal definition not provided in the accessible text.

**Activation-based (from Query stage):**
4. **Last Layer Representation** -- Hidden state from the final transformer layer
5. **Activation Map** -- Two-step: linear transformation + GELU activation
6. **Activation Entropy** -- `- sum_j p_{l,j->t} log p_{l,j->t}` where `p_{l,j->t} = a_{l,j->t} / sum_k a_{l,k->t}`

**Logit-based (from Generation stage):**
7. **Min Token Probability** -- `min_t(softmax(iota_{l,t}))`
8. **Max Token Rank** -- `max_t(rank(softmax(iota_{l,t})))`
9. **Joint Token Probability** -- `product_t softmax(iota_{l,t})`

Note: The paper names 8 features across three categories, though the enumeration in the HTML yields slightly different counts depending on whether "Joint Token Probability" is counted as a third logit feature or a combined metric.

---

### 5. MODELS USED

- **Llama-2-7B**
- **Vicuna-7B**

---

### 6. DATASETS USED

- **CNN/Daily Mail (CNNDM)** -- Summarization task; 286,817 training pairs with ~766-word average source documents
- **HaluEval** -- 5,000 general queries + 30,000 task-specific examples across QA, dialogue, and summarization
- **Natural Questions (NQ)** -- Question-answering; 307,373 training examples (used for transferability experiments)

---

### 7. CLASSIFIERS / METHODS

The paper uses **feature-based static classification** (not temporal methods). The specific classifier type is **not explicitly named** in the accessible text -- the paper describes extracting features and using an `is_halu` function but does not identify whether this is logistic regression, SVM, random forest, or another algorithm. The framework consists of three components:

1. **Internal state extraction** -- extracts states during inference
2. **Token selection** -- selects target tokens for feature extraction
3. **Feature extraction** -- extracts target features from the internal states

**Five token selection strategies** are evaluated:
- **All Tokens**: "Aggregate the features of all tokens (e.g., max, mean) and then input the aggregated result into the is_halu function"
- **First Token**: "Apply the is_halu function only to the first token"
- **Last Token**: "Apply the is_halu function only to the last token"
- **Per Token**: "Apply the is_halu function individually to each token. If any token is identified as hallucinatory, the entire response is considered hallucinatory."
- **Sliced Window**: "Divide all tokens into multiple sliding windows...Apply the is_halu function to each window. If any window is identified as hallucinatory, the entire response is considered hallucinatory." (tested with window sizes 2, 4, 8)

There is **no mention of temporal classification** -- the approach is purely static/per-instance.

---

### 8. KEY FINDINGS

**On attention-based features (the core claim):**

> "Lookback Ratio, an attention-based feature, performs consistently well across both datasets, achieving high accuracy (0.75 on HaluEval and 0.83 on CNNDM) and balanced recall values, suggesting its robustness in both hallucination and factual scenarios."

However, the paper also nuances this:

> "Lookback Ratio is dataset-sensitive, effectively distinguishing hallucinations in CNNDM but not in HaluEval, whereas attention entropy consistently differentiates between hallucinated and factual outputs in both datasets."

And: "Attention entropy robustly captures the dispersion of attention in hallucinated outputs, particularly for HaluEval." The key distinction is that attention entropy showed lower values for factual outputs vs. hallucinations consistently.

**Key experimental results (Llama-2-7B):**

| Feature | HaluEval Acc | CNNDM Acc |
|---|---|---|
| Lookback Ratio | 0.75 | 0.83 |
| Hidden State | 0.76 | 0.74 |
| Joint Probability | 0.54 | 0.63 |

**Token selection strategy performance:**

| Strategy | HaluEval | CNNDM |
|---|---|---|
| Sliced Window (4,2) | 0.87 / 0.89 | 0.85 / 0.87 |
| Per Token | 0.75 | 0.71 / 0.68 |
| All Tokens | 0.51 | 0.52 |

The **Sliced Window (size 4, stride 2)** strategy achieved the best results.

**RAG impact:**
- RAG "enriches attention mechanisms with external knowledge, allowing attention to be allocated across a wider set of tokens"
- RAG increases attention entropy (broader focus)
- RAG "stabilizes activations, reducing variability" and produces "consistently higher" activation values
- Joint token probability increases substantially with RAG, indicating "enhanced cumulative confidence"

**System overhead:**
- Fastest extraction: Last Layer Hidden State (0.09s/token)
- Most expensive: Max Token Ranks (1.15s/token)

---

### 9. LIMITATIONS

The paper identifies these limitations (quoted from the Limitations section):

> "Limited transferability. Based on the transferability experiments and insights from the RAG analysis, it is evident that the internal features of LLMs differ greatly across different scenarios. This lack of consistency results in poor cross-dataset generalizability. For example, features trained on CNNDM fail to perform well on HaluEval and vice versa, highlighting the dataset-specific nature of these features."

Specific transferability numbers: CNNDM-trained models achieved ~0.50 accuracy on HaluEval; CNNDM-to-NQ transfer with Lookback Ratio reached only 0.66.

> "Potential explainability. Despite the limitations, the proposed approach offers a promising avenue for explainability. Attention-based features, such as Lookback Ratio, and logit-based features, such as Joint Token Probabilities, provide interpretable insights into the model's reasoning process."

Additional limitations from the results:
- **Overlapping distributions**: Despite mean differences, feature distributions between hallucinated and factual outputs significantly overlapped
- **Computational overhead**: Some features required O(w * H * L * log w) complexity
- **Only tested on 7B models** (Llama-2-7B and Vicuna-7B) -- no larger models
- **Only an arXiv preprint** -- not peer-reviewed at a venue as of the last version

---

### 10. CONCLUSION (verbatim)

> "In this work, we proposed and evaluated a comprehensive framework for understanding and detecting hallucinations in large language models through internal state analysis. Our experiments demonstrated the potential of using attention, activation, and logit-based features to distinguish between hallucinated and factual outputs. However, challenges remain, including high computational costs, limited transferability of features across datasets, and the need for more efficient and generalizable detection strategies. Despite these limitations, the approach shows promise for improving the explainability of hallucination detection, especially through interpretable features like attention and logits. Future work will focus on optimizing feature extraction for real-time applications and exploring methods to enhance feature transferability across diverse scenarios."

---

### 11. PAPERS CITING HALUPROBE

I conducted extensive searches across arXiv, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, and NASA ADS. **No papers were found that explicitly cite HALUPROBE (arXiv 2502.13490).** I checked the following candidates:

- **LapEigvals** (arXiv 2502.17598) -- spectral features of attention maps for hallucination detection -- does NOT cite HaluProbe
- **HALT** (arXiv 2602.02888) -- log-prob time series for hallucination assessment -- does NOT cite HaluProbe (and explicitly avoids internal state approaches)
- **Hallucination Detection via Internal States and Structured Reasoning Consistency** (arXiv 2510.11529) -- does NOT cite HaluProbe
- **Comprehensive Survey of Hallucination** (arXiv 2510.06265) -- does NOT cite HaluProbe
- **HaloProbe** (arXiv 2604.06165) -- a different paper entirely (Bayesian detection for vision-language models, April 2026); confusingly similar name but unrelated

The paper appears to have very low or zero citations as of May 2026, which is not unusual for a non-venue-published arXiv preprint.

---

### 12. CONTRASTING FINDING FROM RELATED WORK

Notably, a December 2025 empirical study on HuggingFace by krogoldAI found results that **contradict** HaluProbe's claim about attention superiority. Their study found:

- Hidden state activations (FFN output at layer 16): **82.96% accuracy, 91.04% AUC**
- MHA output: 82.11% accuracy, 90.90% AUC
- Attention statistics: 79.90% accuracy, 88.46% AUC

They concluded that "attention features... added no value beyond what FFN activations already provided" and that discriminative information resides "primarily in the feed-forward pathway." This directly challenges HaluProbe's finding that attention-based features are more consistent.

---

### KEY RELATED PAPERS IN THE INTERNAL-STATE HALLUCINATION DETECTION SPACE

- **Lookback Lens** (arXiv 2407.07071) -- the original lookback ratio paper that HaluProbe builds on
- **INSIDE** (2024) -- "LLMs' Internal States Retain the Power of Hallucination Detection"
- **SAPLMA** -- hidden-state-based approach, achieves higher detection than logits/attention in most cases

**Full Title:** "Towards Unification of Hallucination Detection and Fact Verification for Large Language Models"
**Authors:** Weihang Su, Jianming Long, Changyue Wang, Shiyu Lin, Jingyan Xu, Ziyi Ye, Qingyao Ai, Yiqun Liu
**Submitted:** December 2, 2025
**GitHub:** https://github.com/oneal2000/UniFact

---

### 1. Core Contribution: Framework/Benchmark, Not a New Detection Method

UniFact is a **unified evaluation framework and benchmark**, not a new hallucination detection method. Its core contribution is enabling the first direct, instance-level comparison between two previously isolated paradigms:

- **Hallucination Detection (HD):** Model-centric methods that use internal model signals (logits, hidden states, sampling consistency) to detect factual errors.
- **Fact Verification (FV):** Text-centric methods that retrieve external knowledge (e.g., from Wikipedia) and verify claims against retrieved evidence.

These two paradigms had evolved in complete isolation with different assumptions, datasets, and evaluation protocols. UniFact creates a common playing field for head-to-head comparison.

---

### 2. Dynamic Generation and Automatic Labeling Pipeline

UniFact uses a **three-stage dynamic pipeline** rather than static pre-generated outputs:

**Stage 1 -- Dynamic Instance Generation:** A target LLM is prompted with factual questions (sampled from datasets like TriviaQA, NQ, PopQA, etc.) and generates answers in real time. Internal generative signals (token probabilities, hidden states, embeddings) are captured simultaneously. Generation parameters: max 30 new tokens, temperature 0.8, top-p 0.9.

**Stage 2 -- Reference-Based Automated Annotation:** An evaluator model (Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct) receives the tuple (question, generated answer, ground-truth answers, evidence passages) and determines factuality. Human validation showed 97.42% agreement on "hallucination" labels and 99.02% on "non-hallucination" labels.

**Stage 3 -- Unified Evaluation Interface:** Both HD and FV methods predict the same ground-truth factuality labels, but receive different inputs -- HD methods get internal model states while FV methods retrieve from a Wikipedia corpus (DPR corpus, 21 million passages via BM25, top-3 passages).

This design means UniFact can evaluate any LLM dynamically, rather than being locked to a fixed set of pre-generated outputs.

---

### 3. Methods Benchmarked: Both Internal-Signal AND External-Knowledge Methods

This is critical for your question. UniFact compares **both** paradigms:

**White-Box HD Methods (Internal Signals):**
- **LNPP** -- Length-Normalized Predictive Probability (token-level logit signals)
- **LNPE** -- Length-Normalized Predictive Entropy (token-level entropy)
- **SAPLMA** -- Trains a classifier on LLM hidden layer activation values (supervised probe)
- **MIND** -- Uses final-layer token embeddings for unsupervised hallucination detection
- **EUBHD** -- Enhanced uncertainty-based predictive distribution modeling
- **SE** -- Semantic Entropy (token-level entropy + clustering)
- **SEU** -- Semantic Embedding Uncertainty
- **SIndex** -- Inconsistency modeling
- **PTrue** -- Token-level likelihood estimation

**Black-Box HD Methods (Sampling Consistency):**
- **SelfCheckGPT** variants: BertScore, MQA, NLI, N-gram (SCG-BS, SCG-MQA, SCG-NLI, SCG-NG)

**Fact Verification Methods (External Knowledge):**
- **LLM-Q / LLM-QA** -- LLM-based retrieve-then-verify with question-only or question+answer retrieval
- **BERT-Q / BERT-QA** -- BERT NLI classifier with retrieval

**Hybrid Methods:**
- **Score-Level Fusion:** S_hybrid = lambda * S_HD + (1-lambda) * S_FV (with lambda=0.5)
- **Evidence-Aware Pipeline:** FV classifies first; if result is NEI (No Evidence Information), falls back to HD uncertainty signal

---

### 4. Datasets and Models

**Datasets (500 questions sampled from each):**
- TriviaQA (TQA)
- NQ-Open (Natural Questions)
- PopQA (PQA)
- 2WikiMultihopQA (Bridge and Comparison subtypes)
- HotpotQA (Comparison questions)

**Target LLMs evaluated:**
- Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
- Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct

**Judge model:** Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct

---

### 5. Key Quantitative Findings

- **No single paradigm dominates.** The winner fluctuates by dataset and target LLM. HD methods excel on some tasks, FV on others.
- **HD and FV are complementary.** Cross-paradigm complementarity (ACS=0.428) significantly exceeds intra-paradigm complementarity (intra-HD ACS=0.315). Error Correction Rate across paradigms (0.634) also exceeds within-paradigm (0.503).
- **Hybrid methods achieve new SOTA.** Even simple hybrid fusion consistently and significantly outperforms all individual approaches.
- Best individual HD performance: MIND achieved 0.8043 AUC on PopQA (Llama).
- Best individual FV performance: BERT-QA achieved 0.8256 AUC on PopQA (Llama).

---

**Moderate relevance, with important caveats:**

**What is relevant:**
- UniFact does benchmark several internal-signal methods (SAPLMA uses hidden layer activations, MIND uses final-layer embeddings, LNPP/LNPE use logit-derived probabilities/entropy, Semantic Entropy uses token entropy with clustering). This provides a useful baseline comparison for how these signals perform.
- The framework's dynamic evaluation pipeline and automated labeling could be reused or adapted for evaluating new internal-signal methods.
- The finding that internal (HD) and external (FV) methods are complementary is directly relevant -- it suggests internal signals alone capture certain error types but miss others.

**What is NOT covered and limits relevance:**
- **No attention pattern analysis whatsoever.** The paper does not examine attention weights, attention heads, or attention-based features. None of the benchmarked methods use attention signals.
- **No layer-wise / temporal analysis.** There is no investigation of how signals evolve across layers. SAPLMA uses activations from a single (unspecified) layer; MIND uses only the final layer. No intermediate-layer comparison is conducted.
- **No mechanistic interpretability.** There is no eigenvalue decomposition, no probing of individual attention heads, no analysis of information flow through the transformer, no representation geometry analysis.
- **No temporal dynamics.** The framework treats detection as a single-shot classification task on completed outputs, not as a sequential process tracking how hallucination signals build during generation.
- **Only 2 target LLMs** were evaluated (Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B), which limits generalizability claims.

**Bottom line:** UniFact is useful as a well-engineered evaluation harness and for understanding the landscape of existing detection methods, but it operates at a higher level of abstraction than a project focused on comparing internal temporal signals. It tells you *that* internal methods work differently from external ones, but not *which internal representations* (attention vs. hidden states vs. logits across layers) are most informative. A project focused on comparing attention patterns, hidden state evolution, and logit dynamics across layers would be investigating questions UniFact explicitly does not address -- making it complementary background work rather than a direct competitor or framework you would slot into.

Based on the web search results, I found relevant information about TruthfulQA, entity-level hallucination detection, annotation methodologies, and associated limitations:

## Key Findings

**TruthfulQA as a Benchmark:**
TruthfulQA is among major hallucination detection benchmarks including CoQA, TriviaQA, and HaluEval, though most hallucination detection benchmarks operate at the sentence or paragraph level, classifying each generated response as either hallucinated or correct.

**Entity-Level Hallucination Detection Limitations:**
Instance-level detection cannot pinpoint specific hallucinated content, which is crucial for correcting misinformation, and this limitation becomes particularly problematic in long-form text, where a single response often combines supported and unsupported information, making binary quality judgments inadequate.

**Annotation and Methodology Challenges:**
Entity-level annotation is challenging due to its labor-intensive nature, which requires annotators to segment meaningful entities and verify their factuality against reliable sources one by one. Additionally, automated annotation pipelines introduce substantial noise into both training and evaluation data, as LLM judges can make errors when verifying facts, search engines may fail to retrieve relevant evidence for certain claims, and the mapping between claims and entities is sometimes ambiguous.

**Hallucination Onset Detection:**
RIPA identifies both the onset, where the first hallucinated token appears, and the span, the consecutive set of tokens that make up the hallucinated content.

**Detection Method Limitations:**
Uncertainty estimation approaches focusing on individual token probabilities tend to over-predict hallucinations, while context-aware methods show better but still suboptimal performance.

Key changes to make:
1. **HALUPROBE**: Add to landscape and reframe the gap — static comparison exists, temporal comparison doesn't. HALUPROBE's finding is actually contested (krogoldAI found FFN activations beat attention), making the temporal comparison even more needed.

  "title": "TemporalProbe: Which Internal Signal Best Detects Hallucination Onset? A Controlled Comparison of Attention Sinks, Hidden States, and Log-Probabilities as Temporal Features",
  "core_problem": "Multiple internal LLM signals — attention sink scores, hidden-state spectral features, and log-probabilities — have each been independently shown to be effective for hallucination detection when modeled temporally (SinkProbe achieves 23/28 model-dataset wins with static attention sinks; EigenTrack reaches 0.82–0.94 AUROC with GRU-based hidden-state tracking; HALT detects hallucination via GRU on log-probability time series; HSAD gains >10 AUROC points via FFT on cross-layer hidden signals). Yet these results are incomparable: each method uses different architectures, training data, evaluation protocols, and model-benchmark combinations. HALUPROBE (arXiv 2502.13490) partially addressed this gap by systematically comparing attention weights, hidden-state activations, and logits for hallucination detection across three inference stages, finding that 'attention-based features provide more consistent performance across datasets.' However, HALUPROBE's comparison is entirely static — it applies fixed classifiers to per-instance feature snapshots on only two 7B models (Llama-2-7B, Vicuna-7B), and its finding is contested by subsequent work showing FFN activations outperform attention features. More fundamentally, static comparison cannot answer three critical questions that require temporal modeling: (1) which signal enables the earliest detection of hallucination during generation (early-detection curves at partial observation), (2) which signal shows the first distributional shift at hallucination onset (temporal lead/lag analysis), and (3) whether the static ranking (attention > hidden states > logits per HALUPROBE) holds or reverses when signals are modeled as evolving sequences across generation steps. No systematic comparison exists that isolates the signal modality as the independent variable within a temporal framework — training identical temporal classifiers on parallel feature streams extracted from the same generations under the same evaluation protocol. This gap has practical consequences: practitioners building real-time hallucination guardrails must choose a signal type with no principled basis for the choice, and the conflicting static evidence (HALUPROBE favors attention; other studies favor hidden states) cannot be resolved without temporal analysis that reveals when and how each signal becomes informative during generation.",
  "opportunity": "Four independent research threads have converged to make this temporal comparison both possible and timely. (1) Feature identification: SinkProbe (arXiv 2604.10697) established attention sink scores as the strongest attention-based hallucination signal via logistic regression on per-head sink features, using ℓ₁ regularization in its interpretability analysis (Section 4.1) to identify the most informative head-layer combinations. (2) Temporal architecture: EigenTrack (arXiv 2509.15735) and HALT (arXiv 2602.02888) independently proved that lightweight GRU classifiers on per-step internal features achieve strong hallucination detection — but on hidden-state spectral features and log-probabilities respectively, never on attention patterns. (3) Causal grounding: SinkTrack (ICLR 2026) demonstrated that modifying attention sinks causally affects hallucination rates, and FACTUM (arXiv 2601.05866) showed that correct vs. hallucinated citations differ specifically in attention sink usage patterns — establishing that sinks carry independent hallucination-relevant information, not merely downstream reflections of hidden-state dynamics. (4) Static signal comparison: HALUPROBE (arXiv 2502.13490) established the precedent for cross-signal comparison but only with static classifiers on two 7B models, leaving open whether the ranking holds under temporal modeling on modern architectures.

The key insight: these threads define a natural factorial experiment. HALUPROBE showed attention features win statically; we test whether this ranking holds when signals are modeled as temporal sequences during generation. We have three validated signal types (attention sinks, hidden states, log-probs), one validated temporal architecture (GRU), and shared evaluation infrastructure. By training identical GRU classifiers on parallel feature streams extracted from the same model generations, we can isolate the signal modality as the sole independent variable. This controlled temporal comparison — the first of its kind — is the primary contribution. Three outcomes are possible and all are informative: (a) the static ranking holds temporally, validating HALUPROBE's conclusion for real-time deployment; (b) the ranking reverses, revealing that temporal dynamics carry different information than static snapshots; (c) the ranking is task/model-dependent, explaining the contradictory findings across static studies. As part of this comparison, we introduce SinkWatch-GRU, the attention-sink arm that fills the untested cell: a GRU temporal detector consuming per-step attention sink features from SinkProbe's informative heads.",
  "landscape": "**Signal-type comparison for hallucination detection (static):** HALUPROBE (arXiv 2502.13490, Feb 2025) is the most directly related prior work: it systematically compares attention weights, hidden-state activations (FFN outputs), and logits for hallucination detection across three inference stages (understanding/query/generation) on Llama-2-7B and Vicuna-7B, using HaluEval and CNNDM. Key finding: attention-based lookback ratio achieves highest accuracy (0.75 HaluEval, 0.83 CNNDM), with attention entropy showing robust discrimination. However, HALUPROBE has critical limitations: (a) only static classifiers, no temporal modeling; (b) only two older 7B models; (c) limited transferability — CNNDM-trained models achieve ~0.50 on HaluEval; (d) zero venue publications or citations; (e) the finding is contested — a subsequent empirical study (krogoldAI, HuggingFace Dec 2025) found FFN activations (82.96% accuracy, 91.04% AUC) outperform attention statistics (79.90%, 88.46% AUC), concluding attention 'added no value beyond what FFN activations already provided.' This contradiction motivates temporal comparison: the static ranking may depend on the model, dataset, or temporal context of evaluation. UniFact (arXiv 2512.02772, Dec 2025) provides a unified evaluation framework comparing hallucination detection (internal signals) vs. fact verification (external knowledge), benchmarking SAPLMA (hidden states), MIND (final-layer embeddings), and logit-based methods — but does not compare attention patterns, does not analyze layer-wise signals, and treats detection as single-shot classification without temporal modeling. **No prior work compares signal types under temporal modeling during generation.**

**Attention-based hallucination detection (static):** SinkProbe (arXiv 2604.10697, April 2026) proved sink scores outperform spectral Laplacian eigenvalues in 23/28 model-dataset pairs via logistic regression on attention sink features (AUROC 0.778 on TruthfulQA, 0.890 on HaluEval-QA for Llama-3.1-8B), with ℓ₁-regularized variant used for interpretability to identify informative heads. LapEigvals (EMNLP 2025, arXiv 2502.17598) established spectral attention features as hallucination signals. CHARM (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2509.24770) applies GNNs on attributed attention graphs combining attention and activation features. Spectral Guardrails (arXiv 2602.08082, Feb 2026) achieves 97.7% recall via training-free spectral attention topology analysis. AggTruth (ICCS 2025, arXiv 2506.18628) aggregates attention scores with windowing. TOHA (ACL 2026, arXiv 2504.10063) uses topological divergence on attention graphs. Frequency-Aware Attention (arXiv 2602.18145) shows high-frequency attention energy correlates with hallucination. FACTUM (arXiv 2601.05866) uses attention sink usage as one of four mechanistic signals. **All compute features from static snapshots; none model attention feature trajectories across generation steps.**

**Temporal/trajectory hallucination analysis:** Hallucination as Trajectory Commitment (arXiv 2604.15400, April 2026) provides causal evidence that residual-stream trajectories bifurcate at the first generated token in 44.3% of prompts on Qwen2.5-1.5B, with asymmetric attractor dynamics — but tested only residual-stream activations on a single small model, not attention patterns. Before the First Token (arXiv 2604.13068) demonstrates scale-dependent emergence of hallucination signals at position zero. Hallucination Basins (arXiv 2604.04743) formalizes hallucination as trajectory capture in latent-space basins. HalluSAE (arXiv 2604.16430) models hallucination as phase transitions in latent dynamics via sparse autoencoders. Attractor Geometry (arXiv 2605.05686, May 2026) models facts as attractor basins in hidden-state space. First Hallucination Tokens (arXiv 2507.20836) shows the first hallucinated token is far more detectable. Shadows in the Attention (arXiv 2505.16894) reveals an 'attention-locking' threshold (JS-Drift ~0.69) — but tracks drift across prompt perturbation rounds, not generation steps. Step-Level Hallucination Detection via Hidden-State Transport Geometry (arXiv 2605.13772, May 2026) frames hallucination as localized excursion in transport cost along hidden-state trajectories, using BiLSTM on geometric transition features — exclusively on hidden states, not attention. **All study residual-stream or mixed-modality dynamics; none systematically compare signal modalities under controlled conditions.**

**Temporal feature tracking for detection (methods):** EigenTrack (arXiv 2509.15735, 2025) tracks temporal spectral dynamics of hidden-state covariance via GRU (0.82–0.94 AUROC). HALT (arXiv 2602.02888, Feb 2026) treats log-probs as time series via bidirectional GRU (hidden_dim=256, 5 layers). HSAD (arXiv 2509.13154, Sep 2025) applies FFT to cross-layer hidden-state activations, achieving 82.5% AUROC on TruthfulQA and 92.1% on TriviaQA for Qwen-2.5-7B — conceptually related but models vertical dynamics (across layers within a single step) rather than horizontal dynamics (across generation steps). TDGNet (arXiv 2602.08048) targets diffusion language models only. ICR Probe (ACL 2025, arXiv 2507.16488) tracks cross-layer hidden-state evolution (0.73–0.84 AUROC). **Each validates temporal modeling for one signal type but no paper compares signal types under identical temporal architectures.**

**Real-time/online detection:** MIND (ACL Findings 2024, arXiv 2403.06448) is the foundational real-time internal-state detector: an unsupervised framework using last-layer contextualized embeddings with an MLP, achieving passage-level AUC 0.89–0.96 with only 3.3% overhead — but operates post-generation on the final hidden state, uses no temporal modeling, and does not leverage attention patterns. PCNet/PC-LDCD (arXiv 2605.05953, May 2026) trains probabilistic circuits on hidden-state residual stream for online detection; on TruthfulQA specifically, PCNet achieves 0.66–0.81 AUROC across models (0.75±0.06 for Llama-3.1-8B), substantially lower than its 0.95–0.98 AUROC on CoQA/SQuAD — highlighting that TruthfulQA poses a harder detection challenge where improved methods are most needed. RAUQ (arXiv 2505.20045) identifies 'uncertainty-aware' attention heads and recurrently aggregates weights for sequence-level uncertainty — uses simple aggregation (not learned temporal model), targets generic attention (not sinks), operates at sequence granularity. DRIFT (arXiv 2601.14210) trains lightweight probes on hidden states (<0.1% overhead, SOTA on 10/12 settings). Real-Time Entity Detection (arXiv 2509.03531) achieves AUC 0.90 via linear probes on hidden states. Streaming Hallucination Detection (arXiv 2601.02170) treats step-level hallucination as evolving latent state. Monitoring Decoding (ACL Findings 2025, arXiv 2503.03106) uses external reference model logits with 5.7× overhead. **All use hidden-state, logit, or generic attention features; none apply learned temporal models to attention sink features, and none compare signal modalities.**

**Attention sink context:** Attention Sink Survey (arXiv 2604.10098) reviews 180+ papers. SinkTrack (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2604.10027) converts passive attention sinks into active context anchors — demonstrating causal relevance. TARAC (arXiv 2504.04099) tracks visual attention decay in VLMs for mitigation. Mirage in the Eyes (USENIX Security 2025, arXiv 2501.15269) exploits sinks for adversarial attacks.

(2) No method applies learned temporal modeling to attention sink features during autoregressive text generation.",
  "approach": "We propose TemporalProbe, a controlled experimental framework for comparing which internal temporal signal — attention sinks, hidden-state spectral features, or log-probabilities — is most informative for detecting hallucination during autoregressive generation. The framework trains identical GRU classifiers on parallel feature streams extracted from the same model generations, isolating the signal modality as the independent variable. We explicitly position this as the temporal extension of HALUPROBE's static comparison: HALUPROBE showed attention features win statically; we test whether this ranking holds, reverses, or becomes task-dependent when signals are modeled as temporal sequences during generation. As part of this comparison, we introduce SinkWatch-GRU, the first learned temporal detector on attention sink features, filling the untested cell in the comparison.

**What Temporal Comparison Uniquely Reveals Beyond Static Comparison.** Three analyses are impossible with static classifiers and constitute our primary novel contributions over HALUPROBE: (1) Early-detection curves: AUROC as a function of the fraction of the response observed (at 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of tokens) — revealing which signal enables detection earliest, critical for real-time guardrails. (2) Temporal lead/lag analysis: measuring when each signal first shows significant distributional shift relative to annotated hallucination onset — determining whether attention sinks, hidden states, or log-probs are leading or lagging indicators. (3) Complementarity dynamics: whether signals that are redundant in static snapshots carry orthogonal information when modeled temporally (e.g., attention sinks may drift gradually while log-probs shift abruptly, providing complementary temporal signatures).

**Experimental Framework: Three Parallel Arms.** For each generation, we extract three parallel feature streams at every decoding step t:

*Arm 1 — SinkWatch (Attention Sinks):* Per-step features from the top-K informative head-layer combinations (K=5–15) identified via SinkProbe's ℓ₁-regularized interpretability analysis: (a) sink scores for top-k sink tokens (k=2–3), (b) sink concentration (max sink / total sink), (c) sink entropy, (d) context-attention ratio. Augmented with first-order temporal derivatives. Dimensionality ~50–120.

*Arm 2 — EigenTrack-style (Hidden States):* Per-step spectral features from sliding-window covariance matrices of hidden-state activations: leading eigenvalues, spectral gaps, entropy, and RMT statistics. Matching EigenTrack's feature design.

*Arm 3 — HALT-style (Log-Probabilities):* Per-step log-probability features: token log-prob, predictive entropy, top-k probability gap, rank. Matching HALT's feature design.

All three streams feed into identical unidirectional GRUs (hidden_dim=64, ~25K parameters each), trained with identical binary cross-entropy loss, hyperparameters, and data splits. This controlled design isolates the feature modality — same architecture, same training data, same evaluation.

**Primary Analysis: Cross-Signal Comparison.** (1) Detection performance: AUROC and AUPRC for each signal arm at sequence level. (2) Early-detection curves: AUROC as a function of the fraction of the response observed (at 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of tokens), testing which signal enables earliest detection. (3) Temporal lead/lag analysis: measuring when each signal first shows significant distributional shift relative to annotated hallucination onset. (4) Complementarity: late-fusion ensemble combining all three streams to test whether signals carry redundant or orthogonal information; mutual information analysis between per-step predictions from each arm. (5) Static-vs-temporal ranking comparison: explicitly comparing the signal ranking from our temporal GRUs against HALUPROBE's static ranking and against static logistic regression baselines on the same features, to test whether temporal modeling changes the winner. (6) Ablation: SinkWatch-GRU vs. SinkWatch-LR (logistic regression on windowed features) to quantify the benefit of learned temporal modeling over simple aggregation.

**Temporal Characterization (Supporting Analysis).** Statistical tests (paired t-test, Kolmogorov-Smirnov) on sink feature distributions at and before annotated hallucination onset points for 500 examples with hallucination onset annotation. This provides the first empirical evidence on whether attention sink features exhibit gradual drift (enabling temporal detection) or abrupt bifurcation (matching the Trajectory Commitment paper's finding for residual-stream activations).

**Entity-Match Annotation Limitations and Mitigation.** We acknowledge that TruthfulQA contains many nuanced factual claims (e.g., 'What happens if you swallow gum?') where entity-match onset annotation is unreliable — correct answers involve reasoning about consequences, not entity identification. This limitation affects the temporal lead/lag analysis (which requires token-level onset annotation) but NOT the primary cross-signal comparison (which uses sequence-level NLI labels). We mitigate this in three ways: (1) For the EMNLP short paper, we restrict temporal lead/lag analysis to a curated subset of ~300 TruthfulQA questions with clear entity-based answers (e.g., 'Who invented X?', 'What is the capital of Y?'), reporting coverage and selection criteria. (2) We supplement entity-match with NLI-based sliding-window annotation: an NLI model evaluates each sliding window of generated tokens against the gold reference, and onset is defined as the first window where entailment drops below threshold. (3) We report the agreement rate between entity-match and NLI-window onset annotations on the curated subset to quantify annotation reliability. For the AAAI full paper, we add TriviaQA (where entity matching is more reliable for factoid questions) as the primary benchmark for temporal lead/lag analysis.

**Pilot Design and Explicit Decision Rule (First 48 hours).** Before full-scale experiments, run a 2-hour pilot on 100 TruthfulQA examples with Llama-3.1-8B: extract per-step sink features, plot distributions for factual vs. hallucinated tokens at generation fractions (25/50/75/100%). **Decision rule:** If the pilot shows that sink features bifurcate abruptly at the first generated token (matching arXiv 2604.15400's findings for residual stream in ≥70% of examples), then temporal GRU modeling may offer no advantage over static SinkProbe for the sink arm specifically. In this case, we (a) proceed with the cross-signal comparison as the primary contribution (which remains novel and valuable regardless), (b) report the abrupt-bifurcation finding as an empirical result extending arXiv 2604.15400 from residual-stream to attention-sink signals, and (c) investigate whether hidden-state or log-prob arms still benefit from temporal modeling (creating an informative asymmetry across signal types). The paper's contribution is resilient: even if SinkWatch-GRU ≈ static SinkProbe, the controlled cross-signal temporal comparison and the early-detection curves remain the first of their kind.

**Intervention (Extension, AAAI 2027 only).** When the best-performing arm's running probability exceeds a high-confidence threshold, trigger DoLa contrastive decoding for subsequent tokens. Evaluate hallucination rate reduction.

**Dual-Target Venue Strategy:**

*EMNLP 2026 (ARR May 25 — short paper, 4 pages):* Radically descoped. 1 model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), 1 benchmark (TruthfulQA, matching SinkProbe), 1K examples, entity-match onset annotation on curated subset + NLI sequence-level labels. Focus: cross-signal comparison (3 arms) + SinkWatch-GRU vs. static SinkProbe + early-detection curves + static-vs-temporal ranking comparison against HALUPROBE's findings. Key result: which temporal signal is strongest/earliest for hallucination detection, and whether the static ranking holds. No intervention experiments, no 70B model.

*AAAI 2027 (full paper, 8 pages):* Complete framework. 3 models (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Llama-3.1-70B), 3 benchmarks (TruthfulQA, TriviaQA, HaluEval-QA), 2K examples per pair. Full cross-signal comparison, temporal characterization, complementarity analysis, DoLa intervention, temporal lead/lag on TriviaQA (where entity-match is more reliable), comprehensive ablations.

**Training and Evaluation.** Generate outputs, annotate with binary factual/hallucinated labels via NLI against gold references (validated by manual spot-check of 200 examples), split 70/15/15. For EMNLP short paper: NLI-based sequence-level annotation + entity-match onset annotation on curated TruthfulQA subset.

**Baselines.** Static: SinkProbe, LapEigvals, TOHA. Temporal: EigenTrack, HALT. Online: MIND (unsupervised hidden-state), DRIFT, RAUQ, PCNet. Static signal comparison: HALUPROBE-style logistic regression on each feature type (our replication). Ablation: SinkWatch-LR.

**Evaluation Metrics.** Primary: AUROC and AUPRC. Secondary: early-detection AUROC at partial observation, F1 at calibrated threshold, latency overhead (ms/token), mutual information between arms. For intervention (AAAI only): hallucination rate reduction and fluency preservation.",
